Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I feel isolated and set apart from others
I should have protected others and I failed

vignette: Arun, a 35-year-old South Asian tax consultant in suburban Chicago, first remembers the day the war-zone relief mission collapsed like a mirage of smoke and grief. A convoy of aid trucks was ambushed just outside a refugee camp, and the air, thick with diesel fumes, carried the metallic scent of burning. He saw men-tired, face-painted with soot-running for cover while his own hands trembled as he handed out blankets. The memory was chaotic, a blur of screaming, the crunch of broken glass, the sight of a young boy clutching a charred teddy bear. After the mission ended, Arun's life at the office seemed ordinary, but the smell of smoke from a nearby fire in a downtown building would suddenly bring the sound of a siren and the flash of gunfire to his mind. That olfactory trigger would send his heart racing, and he would instinctively cover his face with both hands, hurrying from the conference room, then retreating to his cubicle as if fleeing a battlefield. Even the gentle clatter of a colleague's pencil would make him jump, a startle response that was no longer limited to war memories but had spread to ordinary office sounds. When a client's wife called to discuss a tax filing she had died, Arun would avoid the call, fearing that the funeral conversation would awaken the funeral trigger-funerals, graves, grief-related events-leaving him in a state of constant vigilance. The triggers, therefore, pushed him to adopt maladaptive strategies: avoiding the event site of the convoy, hiding his face in public, and shunning any positive event that might bring a moment of hope. These strategies were not merely responses; they reshaped Arun's worldview. He felt a deep, unshakeable sense of failure-"I should have protected them," he told himself-an appraisal that shattered his long-held belief that he could help those in distress. The sense of isolation grew as he stayed away from team meetings, avoiding the very place where he could have found comfort. The shame that followed each memory was intense, so much so that whenever he recalled the convoy, his body automatically shifted into the cramped, tense posture he had adopted during the ambush, a bodily reenactment that compounded the sense that he had not lived up to his duty. The memories, fragmented and disordered, reinforced the belief that he had failed. Negative appraisals thus fueled the very strategies that kept him numb and distant, while simultaneously heightening his threat perception: his concentration faltered, his nights were plagued by a sense of insecurity that the darkness held danger, and everyday sounds would trigger an adrenaline surge. Threat, in turn, looped back to memory. The constant vigilance made it harder for Arun to sleep; the lack of rest meant that fleeting, intrusive images of the convoy would surface in the middle of the night, bringing with them the shame and bodily tension that had always accompanied them. The same threat that kept him on edge also kept him from confronting the memories-he was so terrified that, when a familiar scent appeared, he would immediately flee, reinforcing the cycle. Even the threat that he might encounter anger-whether from a coworker's exasperated sigh or a friend's frustrated outburst-made him wary, so that the expression of anger itself became a trigger, a cue that the threat was present, causing him to withdraw and cover his face. The avoidance strategies themselves fed the cycle. By consistently avoiding the convoy site-now represented by any crowded or chaotic setting-Arun prevented the disintegration of the memory that could have provided an opportunity to process it. Each time he avoided a positive event, he felt deeper isolation, further entrenching his belief that he was separate from others. Covering his face whenever a smell of smoke rose from a cafeteria or a funeral procession was not just a reflex; it was a shield that reinforced his perception of threat. These strategies amplified the memory's intensity; every time he hid, the body replayed the cramped, tense stance, heightening the shame and the sense of having failed. Each avoidance also reinforced the trigger itself; the more he ignored the smell, the more it became a signal that danger was near, a reminder that the threat was still alive. It was this relentless tightening of the loop that finally pushed Arun to seek help. After months of missing deadlines, struggling to focus on quarterly tax reports, and enduring the constant hum of fear, he woke up one night to the realization that his life had been reduced to a series of escapes. He was terrified of becoming a liability to his clients and his family, of never again feeling the warmth of a shared meal. Yet he also held a fragile hope that, if he could break the cycle, he might return to a life where the scent of smoke would not ignite the ghost of a failed mission. In the therapy room, Arun articulated his greatest fear: that the world would never feel safe again. At the same moment, he clung to the tiny glimmer of possibility-that he could learn to face the triggers, process the memories, and rebuild the shattered beliefs that had kept him locked in a prison of avoidance.
